absent: Semantics of timestamp application when the time vector is null and permission checks inside the timestamp helper.
Behavior of shared timerfd set and query helpers and layout of native and legacy timer structures.
Filesystem attribute handler implementations and their error contracts beyond unsupported and retry indications.
Security-module hook effects, delegation break and wait mechanics, and mount write and audit behavior.
Lookup flag meanings beyond follow and revalidation and stale-detection conditions.
Numeric ABI values for at flags, attribute flags and size maxima and layouts of attribute context and argument structures.

findings.text: Timerfd 32-bit compatibility shims translate between a legacy 32-bit timer specification representation and the native 64-bit form, delegating actual arming and query work to shared helpers. User fetch or store failures are reported as memory faults while helper failures propagate unchanged, and the query variant only writes back on success.

Utimes dispatch selects fd-based handling when pathname is null with a non-default dirfd and otherwise uses pathname handling. A null timestamp vector is forwarded as null, and a vector marking both entries omit completes immediately without filesystem access.

Path timestamp update honors only nofollow and empty-path controls and rejects other flag bits. Trailing symlink following is enabled exactly when nofollow is absent, and stale lookup failures cause one revalidated retry.
Descriptor timestamp update accepts no flag bits and requires a valid open file reference. Any flag use or an empty descriptor fails without further action.

Legacy timeval timestamp inputs have their microsecond fields range checked before conversion, with out-of-range values rejected. Valid values keep seconds and scale microseconds to nanosecond resolution for the internal pair.

Legacy futimesat, utimes, utime and 32-bit time aliases normalize seconds-only or timeval user forms into a two-entry timestamp pair, using zero subsecond parts where the source has none, then invoke shared dispatch with fixed directory and flag defaults.
Attribute sort key holds a pointer to a parent list head plus a name string pointer, expressing membership without owning storage.

Attribute access control reports write denials differently from read denials, leaves security and system namespaces to lower layers, gates the trusted namespace on administrative privilege, limits the user namespace by file kind with an extra ownership check for sticky directories, and otherwise defers to generic inode permission.
User namespace support probe fails closed when the inode lacks attribute operations or is bad, and otherwise succeeds exactly when at least one registered handler advertises the user prefix.

Unpermissioned attribute set clears the no-security marker for security names, prefers the filesystem handler when available with change notification and post handling on success, and otherwise only for security names attempts a security-module store with notification.

Locked attribute set and remove require successful permission and security authorization plus delegation release before invoking low-level mutation. Any denial aborts without mutation or notification.

Attribute set and remove hold the target inode lock across the whole authorization and mutation attempt, release it before waiting for delegation recall, and repeat the attempt after a successful recall wait.
Setting the capability attribute with nonzero size passes through a mount-aware conversion that may replace the value buffer and size. Any replacement buffer is released after the attempt.

Getting a security name authorizes through generic permission and a security hook, then queries the security store with distinct handling for size probes versus sized copies including range enforcement, falling through to the filesystem getter only when no security module claims the name.

Allocating getter resolves the responsible handler after permission, learns value length through a size probe, grows the caller buffer when absent or too small with zeroed extension, then fills it and returns the length.

Listing uses the filesystem list operation when present and otherwise accumulates only security-module names while reporting used bytes. The user wrapper truncates oversized requests to a ceiling and maps an over-ceiling range failure to a too-big error.
Attribute name import from user memory fails with a range error for empty or overlong names and propagates copy faults, preventing unbounded or missing names from reaching lower layers.
Set copy validation rejects flag bits outside create and replace, rejects values beyond the size ceiling, and duplicates user values into kernel memory with allocation failures propagated.
Names recognized as POSIX access control entries are diverted to dedicated access control helpers for set and get instead of the generic attribute path.

Path, file and at-based attribute helpers accept only nofollow and empty-path controls, derive symlink following from nofollow, treat null pathname with a valid descriptor as a file operation, and retry once with revalidation on stale lookups. Write paths additionally require mount write access with auditing.

User-facing get caps oversized requests to the value ceiling for allocation, copies out only on positive length with fault detection, and maps a range failure at or above the ceiling to a too-big error.

Portable set, get and list entries are thin adapters over at-variants with fixed directory and follow behavior, including nofollow and descriptor-based forms. Extensible-argument forms bound the argument struct size, copy it from user, reject nonzero get flags, and unpack value pointer, size and flags.

Delegation handling is a loop with attempt-under-lock and wait-without-lock states. A delegated indication leads to a recall wait and re-entry into attempt, exiting on a non-delegated result or wait failure.
Path lookup is a lookup-use-release loop. A stale indication adds revalidation and repeats lookup, otherwise the first outcome stands.
User time, name, value and list pointers are untrusted. Copy or fetch failures surface as faults and invalid numeric fields or flag combinations as invalid, without partial mutation.
Timestamp vectors carry two entries for access and modification. Marking both entries omit short-circuits update, and legacy timeval entries use microsecond units bounded below one million.

Attribute creation distinguishes create-only from replace-only modes, lookup distinguishes nofollow from empty-path behavior, and value and list sizes are bounded by dedicated maxima whose overflow surfaces as too-big.
